title: MODULE 04 — Responsive Design, Accessibility and UI Engineering

overview.text: This module teaches students how to engineer interfaces that remain usable, consistent, accessible, and visually reliable across different devices, screen sizes, and interaction methods.

After completing Module 03, students understand CSS, Flexbox, Grid, positioning, responsive units, and component styling. This module takes those skills further by applying them to real-world interface engineering.
The focus shifts from how to style individual elements to how to design, build, test, and maintain complete user interfaces for different people and environments.

Important distinction: Module 03 teaches the CSS technologies. Module 04 teaches how to apply those technologies to real responsive products, implement accessibility requirements, establish design systems, and develop reusable interface components.
Learning Outcomes
By completing this module, students should be able to:
Design responsive and adaptive interfaces based on actual content and user requirements.
Apply mobile-first development principles.
Select appropriate media-query and container-query strategies.
Build fluid layouts and responsive typography.
Engineer consistent experiences across mobile, tablet, laptop, and desktop.
Understand WCAG accessibility principles and conformance levels.
Implement keyboard navigation and predictable focus management.
Understand screen reader behavior, accessible names, ARIA roles, and component semantics.
Evaluate color contrast and design inclusive interfaces.
Build design systems using design tokens and standardized components.
Create reusable buttons, navigation, cards, dialogs, forms, and interface patterns.
Test responsive behavior and accessibility systematically.
Standards foundation: The accessibility lessons use WCAG 2.2 as the primary reference. W3C recommends using WCAG 2.2 for current and future-oriented accessibility work.
W3C
Module Overview
Modern frontend engineering requires creating interfaces that work reliably across different devices, browsers, screen sizes, and user interaction methods.

A website that looks perfect on a desktop but breaks on a mobile phone is not a complete frontend implementation. Similarly, a visually attractive application that cannot be navigated using a keyboard or understood by screen readers is not a professionally engineered interface.
This module focuses on three interconnected disciplines:
Responsive Engineering: Building interfaces that adapt to different screen sizes, device characteristics, and available space.
Accessibility Engineering: Making interfaces usable by people with different visual, auditory, motor, and cognitive abilities.
UI Engineering: Creating reusable components, consistent design systems, and predictable interaction patterns.
Learning Outcomes
By the end of this module, students should be able to:
Design responsive interfaces using content-driven breakpoints.
Implement mobile-first and adaptive design strategies.
Combine media queries and container queries effectively.
Create fluid layouts and scalable typography.
Design interfaces for mobile, tablet, desktop, and wide screens.
Understand WCAG 2.2 and its accessibility conformance levels.
Implement keyboard navigation and accessible focus behavior.
Understand screen readers and accessibility trees.
Apply ARIA roles, states, and properties appropriately.
Evaluate color contrast and interface usability.
Build design systems with primitive, semantic, and component design tokens.
Develop reusable buttons, navigation bars, cards, dialogs, and forms.
Establish component states, variants, interaction contracts, and accessibility requirements.
Perform responsive, keyboard, and accessibility testing.

sections.title: LESSON 01 — Responsive and Adaptive Design Principles

blocks.text: Responsive web design is an approach to building websites that adjust their presentation and layout according to the available screen space and viewing environment.
A responsive website should remain useful when viewed on:
Consider an educational platform containing a navigation bar and a collection of course cards.
On a desktop, the layout may display three course cards in one row.
On a tablet, it may display two cards per row.
On a mobile device, it may display one card per row.
The information remains the same, but the layout changes to provide a suitable experience.
The purpose is not simply to shrink the desktop design. It is to make the interface adapt to the available space without sacrificing usability or important functionality.
Responsive design commonly combines three techniques.
Elements use flexible dimensions that adapt to available space.
The container expands when space is available but maintains a maximum width.
Images and videos adapt to their containers.
The layout changes when the viewport meets defined conditions.

.course-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); } @media (max-width: 800px) { .course-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } } @media (max-width: 550px) { .course-grid { grid-template-columns: 1fr; } }
These techniques work together to create responsive interfaces.
Adaptive design uses selected layout configurations for different device or viewport conditions.
Instead of continuously adjusting every component, an adaptive design may use a limited number of predefined configurations.
On a desktop, the application might display:
A menu that opens when requested.
The interface is adapted according to the available space and interaction requirements.
Desktop sidebar replaced by mobile drawer
Modern applications frequently combine both approaches.
For example, a dashboard may use a fluid responsive content area while changing its sidebar into a mobile navigation drawer at a chosen breakpoint.
1.5 The Three Major Responsive Design Questions
How much horizontal and vertical space is available?
Does the current layout provide enough room for text, buttons, images, and navigation?
Can users comfortably interact with the interface using their available input methods?
A design decision should not be based only on screen dimensions.
For example, a tablet in landscape orientation may have enough space for a desktop-style navigation bar, while the same tablet in portrait orientation may require a different layout.
A common mistake is choosing breakpoints only because a device belongs to a particular category.
Instead, choose breakpoints when the content or layout stops working comfortably.
.navigation { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; } @media (max-width: 760px) { .navigation { flex-direction: column; align-items: stretch; } }
The breakpoint should be determined by testing the actual navigation content.
It may be 760px in one project and 900px in another.
There is no universal breakpoint for every website.
Responsive layouts require more than responsive containers.
A large image may still download unnecessarily large resources on mobile devices.
Use appropriate image resources and responsive image techniques.
The browser can select an appropriate resource based on the image's rendered size and device conditions.
Navigation is one of the most important elements to adapt.
A desktop navigation might display all links horizontally.
On mobile, the same design might create:
A better mobile arrangement may use a menu button that opens the navigation.
The menu must remain usable with both pointer and keyboard interaction.
Do not simply hide navigation links without giving mobile users an accessible way to reach them.
Too many links in a small space.
Test your implementation at different widths and document every layout change.
Mobile-first development is a design and implementation strategy in which the initial layout is designed for smaller screens before adding enhancements for wider screens.
The approach starts with essential content and functionality.
As more screen space becomes available, the interface progressively introduces additional layout capabilities.
Desktop: Three-column course listing with a sidebar.
This encourages developers to prioritize important information rather than assuming that every interface element must be visible simultaneously.
A mobile-first strategy encourages developers to create layouts that work under tighter constraints.
It also helps prevent a common problem: trying to compress a complex desktop interface into a small viewport without redesigning its structure.
Start with the smallest practical layout.

@media (min-width: 700px) { .course-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); gap: 20px; } } @media (min-width: 1100px) { .course-grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(3, 1fr); gap: 24px; padding: 32px; } }
The default styles support smaller screens.
Media queries progressively enhance the layout.
Progressive enhancement means establishing a functional foundation and improving the experience when additional capabilities are available.
A learning page should initially provide:
The important content and core functionality should not depend unnecessarily on decorative enhancements.
Mobile interfaces require careful attention to how users interact with elements.
A small icon button may be easy to click using a mouse but difficult to activate accurately on a touchscreen.
.icon-button { min-width: 44px; min-height: 44px; display: inline-flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }
This creates a reasonably sized interaction target.

WCAG 2.2 Level AA defines a 24-by-24 CSS pixel minimum target-size criterion with specified exceptions. A 44-by-44 CSS pixel target is the enhanced Level AAA criterion, also subject to its exceptions.
Designing larger controls where practical improves usability, especially on mobile interfaces.
Desktop interfaces often use hover to reveal information.
This is insufficient as the only interaction method.
Touch users may not have a conventional hover interaction, and keyboard users need another way to reveal the same information.
A better approach uses explicit controls:
Frontend Engineering
JavaScript controls whether the additional options are visible.
The control's state must be updated consistently.
Mobile layouts should prioritize essential content.
For example, a course card may display:
A larger desktop layout may additionally display:
Do not remove essential information merely to make the mobile layout fit.
Reorganize content rather than unnecessarily hiding important functionality.
Forms should be optimized for smaller screens.
.form { display: grid; gap: 20px; width: min(100%, 520px); } .form input, .form select, .form textarea { width: 100%; min-width: 0; padding: 12px; }
A design that works at 375px width may still fail when a user increases text size or rotates the device.
Take a desktop-oriented course dashboard and redesign it using a mobile-first strategy.
Extend the layout for tablets and desktops without duplicating the entire application.

sections.title: LESSON 03 — Media Queries and Container Queries

blocks.text: Media queries allow developers to apply styles conditionally based on characteristics of the output environment.
The most common use is responsive viewport styling.
The rule applies when the viewport meets the defined condition.
Media queries can also respond to:
min-width applies a rule at or above a specified width.
max-width applies a rule at or below a specified width.
Mobile-first projects commonly use min-width queries.
This applies between the specified viewport-width boundaries.
The orientation feature can respond to portrait or landscape orientation.
Orientation should not be treated as a reliable substitute for measuring available space.
A small phone in landscape mode may still require a compact layout.
Different devices have different pointing capabilities.
This applies hover enhancements when the primary input can hover and has a fine pointing mechanism.
You can also use any-hover and any-pointer when considering all available input mechanisms rather than only the primary one.
Do not make hover the only way to perform an action.
The user's operating system may indicate a preferred color scheme.
A website can also provide an explicit theme control.
Respecting system preferences and supporting a user-controlled theme are complementary strategies.
Users may configure their systems to reduce nonessential movement.
Motion preferences should be considered when designing loading indicators, scroll effects, transitions, and animated controls.
Media queries respond to environmental characteristics such as the viewport.
Container queries allow a component to respond to the size of its containing element.
This is especially useful for reusable components that may appear in different layout contexts.
In a wide content area, the image and text can appear side by side.
In a narrow sidebar, the same card should become vertically stacked.
A viewport media query may not solve this because the viewport could remain wide while the card's own container becomes narrow.
This establishes a named query container for its descendants.
The inline-size containment is often appropriate for components responding to available width.
.course-card { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 1fr; gap: 16px; } @container courses (min-width: 600px) { .course-card { grid-template-columns: 180px 1fr; align-items: center; } }
When the courses container reaches the defined inline size, the component changes its layout.
The cqi unit represents a percentage of the relevant query container's inline size.
Use container-query units only when a suitable query container exists.
Change card arrangement inside a narrow panel
A professional application often uses both.
A sidebar that changes behavior on smaller screens.
A course card responding to its own container width.
A grid of reusable components in different containers.
Hover enhancements for suitable pointer devices.
Document why each change uses a media query or a container query.

sections.title: LESSON 04 — Fluid Layouts and Responsive Typography

blocks.text: A fluid layout uses flexible measurements that adapt as available space changes.
Instead of assigning every section a fixed width, developers use relative dimensions and constraints.
The container grows when more space is available and stops expanding at 1200px.
Fluid layouts reduce the need for unnecessary breakpoint-specific adjustments.
This may overflow on a narrower screen.
The second layout adapts to its containing space.
A responsive course grid can use:
.course-grid { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(min(100%, 260px), 1fr)); gap: 24px; }
The grid creates as many columns as the available width allows.
Each card has a preferred minimum size while remaining flexible.
The inner min() prevents the minimum track size from forcing the grid beyond an extremely narrow container.
Section spacing should also adapt to different screen sizes.
This allows spacing to increase naturally as viewport width grows.
A large heading that works on desktop may overflow a mobile screen.
Responsive typography uses flexible text sizes and constraints.
The minimum keeps the heading readable.
The preferred value scales with the viewport.
The browser uses a different font.
The content is longer than expected.
Avoid rigid height constraints on text containers.
Longer text may become inaccessible or visually truncated.
When text must be truncated for a particular product design, provide a way to access the complete information.
A page containing technical lessons should not stretch long paragraphs across an extremely wide screen.
This creates a centered reading column with flexible width.

WCAG 2.2 Level AA includes a reflow requirement for most content at a width equivalent to 320 CSS pixels, without loss of information or functionality and without requiring two-dimensional scrolling, except for content that inherently requires two-dimensional presentation.
This matters because users may reach a narrow effective viewport by zooming rather than using a physically small device.

Developers should test actual content reflow rather than assuming that a page is accessible merely because it looks good on a standard phone. W3C defines the detailed reflow requirements and exceptions in WCAG 2.2.
This allows image dimensions to adapt while maintaining a consistent visual ratio.
For logos and diagrams, object-fit: contain may be more suitable than cover.

.dashboard { width: min(100% - 32px, 1440px); margin-inline: auto; display: grid; grid-template-columns: minmax(0, 1fr); gap: clamp(16px, 3vw, 32px); } .dashboard-title { font-size: clamp(24px, 3vw, 40px); } @media (min-width: 900px) { .dashboard { grid-template-columns: 240px minmax(0, 1fr); } }
The layout remains fluid while adapting its major structure at a content-appropriate breakpoint.

sections.title: LESSON 05 — Designing for Mobile, Tablet and Desktop

blocks.text: Responsive engineering is not just about fitting elements into smaller containers.
Different devices can produce different interaction and layout requirements.
A mobile interface is often operated with touch.
A desktop interface may be operated with a mouse and keyboard.
A tablet can support touch input, keyboards, trackpads, and different orientations.
An effective design system must support these differences without creating inconsistent experiences.
A single-column layout is often suitable for content-heavy mobile applications.
Tablets provide more available space than mobile phones but may not provide enough width for a complete desktop arrangement.
The sidebar and main content can now coexist.
Desktop layouts can provide more complex information structures.
.dashboard { display: grid; grid-template-columns: 260px minmax(0, 1fr); gap: 32px; max-width: 1440px; margin-inline: auto; padding: 32px; }
A large content area can contain several columns, while the sidebar remains visible.
However, wider screens should not automatically produce wider paragraphs and unlimited content widths.
Use maximum-width constraints and intentional information hierarchy.
Useful for desktop interfaces with sufficient room.
Useful when navigation links no longer fit comfortably.
A panel that opens when the user activates a menu button.
Can be appropriate for applications with a small number of frequently used primary destinations.
Navigation choices should depend on the application's information architecture, not just visual trends.
Tables may need special treatment on smaller screens.
Horizontal scrolling for genuinely tabular data.
Hiding nonessential supplementary columns only when their information remains available.
Presenting an alternative compact view where appropriate.
Providing meaningful row and column headers.
Do not blindly convert every table into unrelated cards if doing so removes important data relationships.
A dialog that appears in the center of a large desktop screen may need to become a nearly full-screen panel on mobile.

.dialog { width: min(90vw, 560px); max-height: min(80vh, 700px); overflow-y: auto; border: 0; border-radius: 16px; padding: 24px; } @media (max-width: 600px) { .dialog { width: calc(100% - 24px); max-height: calc(100% - 24px); border-radius: 12px; } }
The dialog must also remain keyboard accessible and ensure that its content and controls are reachable.
Mobile browser toolbars can expand and collapse, changing the available viewport height.
For a panel that should remain usable when mobile browser controls change, test the behavior rather than assuming that traditional 100vh always represents the currently visible area.
Emulation is useful, but it cannot replace testing on real devices.
Take a desktop learning dashboard and create three intentional layouts.
Document the conditions under which each layout is activated and explain why those conditions were selected.

sections.title: LESSON 06 — Accessibility Standards and WCAG Fundamentals

blocks.text: Web accessibility means creating websites and applications that people with different abilities can perceive, understand, navigate, and operate.
Accessibility is not limited to screen readers.
Need additional time to understand or complete a task.
Accessibility improves the usability of the web for everyone.
WCAG stands for Web Content Accessibility Guidelines.
It is a set of internationally recognized accessibility guidelines developed through the World Wide Web Consortium's accessibility work.
WCAG defines testable success criteria for evaluating web content.
The current course reference is WCAG 2.2.
WCAG is organized around four fundamental principles.
6.3 The Four Principles of WCAG — POUR
Users must be able to perceive the information presented.
Provide meaningful alternative text for images.
Avoid relying only on color to communicate information.
Ensure content adapts to different display conditions.
Users must be able to operate the interface.
Avoid interactions that depend exclusively on complex gestures.
Content and interactions should be understandable.
Content should work with different browsers and assistive technologies.
Ensure components expose their current states.
Additional requirements that provide a more comprehensive level of accessibility.
A more demanding set of success criteria.
A project may target WCAG 2.2 Level AA as its general development goal while incorporating additional AAA improvements where practical.

It is important to distinguish a development target from an actual conformance claim. A complete WCAG evaluation must consider the applicable requirements across the relevant scope, not just a few automated checks.
6.5 Important WCAG Criteria for Frontend Engineers
Ensure sufficient contrast for relevant controls
Allow users to move focus away
Do not entirely hide focused components
Provide useful correction suggestions when appropriate
This is a selection of important criteria, not a complete WCAG checklist.
Normal text generally requires at least 4.5:1 contrast.
Large text generally requires at least 3:1 contrast.
Relevant non-text interface components and graphical objects generally require at least 3:1 contrast against adjacent colors.
The guidelines include specific exceptions for certain content and situations.
Contrast should be checked for all important states, including hover, focus, disabled, and selected states where the corresponding criteria apply.
Accessibility testing should be performed at multiple levels.
Check semantic elements, labels, attributes, and DOM structure.
Listen to how content and controls are announced.
Check contrast, focus indicators, text resizing, and layout.
Use tools to detect common accessibility problems.
No single test can prove that an entire website is accessible.
Screen readers such as NVDA, VoiceOver, and TalkBack.
Use automated tools as part of a broader testing process.
An automated report may detect missing accessible names but will not reliably determine whether every label, instruction, or interaction makes sense to a human user.
Audit a previously developed website using WCAG 2.2 as the reference.
Classify the problems according to the relevant WCAG principle and criterion.

sections.title: LESSON 07 — Keyboard Navigation and Focus Management

blocks.text: Keyboard accessibility means users can operate all essential website functionality without relying on a mouse or touchscreen.
Keyboard interaction is particularly important for:
Power users who prefer keyboard navigation.
People temporarily unable to use a pointing device.
A website should not require users to hover, drag, or click with a mouse to access important functionality.
Keyboard focus identifies the control that is currently ready to receive keyboard interaction.
<button type="button"> Start Learning </button> <input type="text" placeholder="Search courses">
When users press Tab, the browser moves focus through focusable elements according to their navigation behavior.
Users should always be able to identify which element has focus visually.
Move to the next focusable element
Move to the previous focusable element
Activate buttons and toggle applicable controls
Dismiss dialogs, menus, and applicable overlays
Move to the beginning of certain composite widgets
Move to the end of certain composite widgets
Exact keyboard behavior depends on the type of interface component.
Native elements already support many of these behaviors.
The tabindex attribute controls keyboard focus participation.
Makes an otherwise non-natively-focusable element focusable in normal sequential keyboard navigation.
Allows programmatic focus but removes the element from the normal sequential Tab order.
Values greater than zero create an artificial focus order and should generally be avoided.
However, making a div focusable does not automatically make it behave like a button.
Do not remove focus outlines without providing an equivalent replacement.
This provides a visible keyboard focus indicator.
Avoid being hidden underneath sticky elements.
Work in both light and dark themes.
Keyboard focus should follow a predictable sequence.

Home Courses

Course Registration
The DOM order should generally reflect the intended reading and interaction sequence.
Using CSS to visually rearrange elements should not create a misleading keyboard or screen reader order.
Traditional multi-page navigation often causes the browser to load a new document.
Single-page applications may change content without a full page reload.
As a result, developers sometimes need to manage focus after navigation.

import { useEffect, useRef } from "react"; function CoursePage() { const headingRef = useRef(null); useEffect(() => { headingRef.current?.focus(); }, []); return (

This example programmatically focuses the page heading when the component mounts.
In production applications, route-change handling should ensure that focus moves at the appropriate time and does not interrupt the user unnecessarily.
Focus should move into the dialog.
Keyboard users should be able to interact with its controls.
Background content should not remain interactable as if the dialog were not open.
Focus should return to the triggering control when the dialog closes, where appropriate.
Native dialog functionality can help implement this behavior.
A custom modal may require focus to remain within the modal while it is active.
However, manually implementing focus trapping is difficult.
Prefer a native modal dialog where its behavior fits the application requirements.
Do not apply focus trapping to ordinary nonmodal panels.
Roving tabindex is a keyboard-navigation technique used inside certain composite widgets.
Instead of allowing every item to receive focus independently through Tab, one item participates in the tab order while arrow keys move focus between items.
This pattern requires deliberate implementation of focus and keyboard state.
Follow the W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide for each widget pattern rather than inventing keyboard behavior.
Test a complete page using only the keyboard.
Focus is not hidden behind sticky navigation or overlays.
Build a keyboard-accessible navigation system and modal interface.
Escape dismisses the dialog where appropriate.
Focus returns to the original trigger.
All actions work without a mouse.

sections.title: LESSON 08 — Screen Readers, ARIA and Accessible Components

blocks.text: A screen reader is assistive technology that communicates information from the user interface through speech or other output.
It allows users to interact with websites without relying on visual presentation.
Screen readers interpret information exposed by the browser's accessibility infrastructure.
The exact announcement depends on the browser, screen reader, interaction mode, and control implementation.
Browsers maintain accessibility information representing elements that are exposed to assistive technologies.
This information is often presented conceptually as an accessibility tree.
The accessibility tree contains information such as:
For example, a button in the DOM:
Has a native button role and an accessible name derived from its text.
A screen reader can announce the control as a button named "Enrol Now."
ARIA stands for Accessible Rich Internet Applications.
It provides semantic attributes that help communicate interface roles, states, properties, and relationships to assistive technologies.
ARIA is particularly useful for custom interactive components.
However, ARIA does not automatically create the behavior of an interactive control.
Roles communicate what an element represents.
Native elements should be preferred whenever an equivalent semantic HTML element already exists.
The native button already provides the expected role and keyboard behavior.
The icon button has an accessible name even though it contains no visible descriptive text.
The label distinguishes this navigation region when other navigation regions exist.
For controls that contain visible text, keep their accessible name aligned with the visible label so speech-input users can identify and activate them correctly.
aria-labelledby connects a component to another element containing its label.
Confirm Enrolment
The heading supplies the dialog's accessible name.
aria-describedby associates supplementary descriptive text with a control.
Use at least eight characters.
This helps assistive technologies communicate the additional instruction.
These attributes are commonly used for expandable components.
Frontend Backend
When the menu opens, JavaScript should update both:
These attributes communicate state and relationships. They do not create the actual open-and-close behavior.
Live regions communicate certain changes that occur without moving focus.
const status = document.querySelector("#form-status"); function announceSuccess() { status.textContent = "Your registration was successful."; }
The browser and assistive technology may announce the changed content according to the live-region behavior.
Do not make every changing element a live region. Excessive announcements can overwhelm users.
aria-hidden="true" removes an element and its descendants from the accessibility tree.
<button type="button"> <svg aria-hidden="true"> <!-- Decorative icon --> </svg> Start Learning </button>
The icon is decorative, while the button text provides the accessible name.
Do not apply aria-hidden="true" to an element that contains content or controls users need to access.
Avoid placing focusable descendants inside content hidden from assistive technologies.
Use native HTML first, then add ARIA when a genuine semantic requirement remains.

The W3C ARIA Authoring Practices Guide provides implementation patterns, keyboard conventions, and functional examples for custom widgets. It is an important resource when building advanced components.
Frontend engineering involves building the interface and user-facing behavior of applications.

const faqButton = document.querySelector(".faq-item button"); const answer = document.querySelector("#faq-answer"); faqButton.addEventListener("click", () => { const isExpanded = faqButton.getAttribute("aria-expanded") === "true"; faqButton.setAttribute( "aria-expanded", String(!isExpanded) ); answer.hidden = isExpanded; });
This creates a simple disclosure pattern.
For a group of independent accordion sections, each control should have its own unique identifiers and associated panel.

The native modal dialog provides important browser-managed behavior, including modal interaction and Escape-key handling.
The method="dialog" form closes the dialog when its button is activated and sets the dialog result.
Ensure the initial focus choice is appropriate.
Restore focus to the opener when necessary.
Prevent accidental dismissal where the task requires it.
Verify screen reader announcements and mobile behavior.
Students should practice using at least one screen reader.
Observe whether the information presented to the screen reader matches the purpose of each interface element.

sections.title: LESSON 09 — Color Contrast and Inclusive Interface Design

blocks.text: Inclusive interface design considers the different ways people perceive and interact with digital products.
It recognizes that users do not all experience a website in the same way.
The aim is to avoid designing around only one assumed user profile.
Color contrast describes the difference in luminance between foreground and background colors.
It affects how easily text and interface components can be distinguished.
Black text on a white background generally provides strong contrast.
Light gray text on a white background may be difficult to read.
A visually attractive palette is not automatically an accessible palette.
WCAG uses contrast ratios to evaluate the relative luminance of foreground and background colors.
Relevant UI components and graphical objects
The standard defines specific exceptions. These values should not be applied blindly to every decorative element.
WCAG defines large-scale text using specific font size and weight conditions.
These correspond to approximately 24 CSS pixels and 18.67 CSS pixels respectively.
Use the actual WCAG definition rather than assuming that every visually large heading qualifies automatically.
9.5 Color Should Not Be the Only Indicator
An error state that only changes a border to red may not be clear to everyone.
Enter a valid email address.
The error is communicated using both a visible border and explanatory text.
Do not rely on green, orange, red, or gray alone.
Use explicit text labels and meaningful icons.

✓ Completed

● In progress
Each state remains understandable even when colors are not distinguishable.
Buttons, form controls, and interaction indicators should remain distinguishable from their surroundings.
A dark button with a subtle border may become difficult to identify on a dark background.
An input field may be difficult to distinguish if its border and background have very similar colors.
Use appropriate contrast testing for each state.
Interfaces should also accommodate users who need different text presentations.
Preserving content when users enlarge text.
The layout should tolerate changes to text spacing without losing functionality.
WCAG 2.2 Level AA includes Target Size (Minimum), requiring pointer targets to be at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels unless a defined exception applies.
Level AAA includes a 44 by 44 CSS pixel enhanced target-size criterion, also with exceptions.
For practical interface engineering, provide larger interactive areas when possible, especially for important mobile controls.
Closely spaced icon buttons should also have sufficient separation.
9.10 Designing for Reduced Motion and Sensory Preferences
Inclusive interface design extends beyond color and typography.
A useful design system should support accessible motion behavior from the beginning.
Create an inclusive design audit for a technology learning platform.
Document each issue and implement an improvement.

sections.title: LESSON 10 — Design Systems, Design Tokens and Component Consistency

blocks.text: A design system is a structured collection of reusable design decisions, standards, components, patterns, and documentation.
It helps teams build interfaces that maintain consistent appearance and behavior across an application.
A design system is more than a color palette or a collection of buttons.
Without a shared system, different developers may implement:
Over time, the application becomes visually inconsistent.
A design system creates shared rules that reduce unnecessary variation.
Design tokens are named values representing reusable design decisions.

:root { /* Colors */ --color-primary: #171717; --color-accent: #d97706; --color-background: #ffffff; --color-surface: #f5f5f5; --color-text: #171717; --color-muted: #666666; /* Spacing */ --space-1: 4px; --space-2: 8px; --space-3: 12px; --space-4: 16px; --space-6: 24px; --space-8: 32px; --space-12: 48px; /* Typography */ --font-body: system-ui, sans-serif; --font-heading: system-ui, sans-serif; --font-size-sm: 0.875rem; --font-size-base: 1rem; --font-size-lg: 1.25rem; /* Borders */ --radius-sm: 6px; --radius-md: 12px; --radius-lg: 20px; /* Motion */ --duration-fast: 150ms; --duration-normal: 250ms; }
These tokens provide a common vocabulary for styling decisions.
Large design systems benefit from multiple token layers.
Semantic tokens describe the purpose of a value.
Component tokens describe styling decisions for specific components.
This separation makes a design system easier to customize and maintain.
10.5 Why Semantic Tokens Are Better Than Scattered Values
A semantic token provides a central definition:
When the design system changes, developers can update the shared token rather than searching through unrelated component files.
A component system should define consistent rules for common interface elements.
For example, every primary button may share:

.button { display: inline-flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center; gap: 8px; min-height: 44px; padding: 10px 18px; border: 1px solid transparent; border-radius: var(--radius-md); font: inherit; font-weight: 600; cursor: pointer; } .button--primary { background: var(--color-action-primary); color: white; } .button--secondary { background: var(--color-surface-main); color: var(--color-text-primary); border-color: #d4d4d4; }
A design system must define not only default appearances but also component states.
.button:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid var(--color-action-primary); outline-offset: 3px; } .button:disabled { opacity: 0.6; cursor: not-allowed; }
However, reduced opacity alone should not be the only way to communicate disabled state.
A design system should support theme-level token changes.

:root, [data-theme="light"] { color-scheme: light; --surface-page: #ffffff; --surface-card: #f5f5f5; --text-primary: #171717; --border-subtle: #e5e5e5; } [data-theme="dark"] { color-scheme: dark; --surface-page: #171717; --surface-card: #262626; --text-primary: #ffffff; --border-subtle: #404040; } body { background: var(--surface-page); color: var(--text-primary); } .card { background: var(--surface-card); border: 1px solid var(--border-subtle); }
Theme changes should be checked for:
A theme is not complete merely because the page background changes.
Every component should have documentation explaining:
For example, a button component may support:

Button │ ├── Variants │ ├── Primary │ ├── Secondary │ ├── Outline │ └── Destructive │ ├── Sizes │ ├── Small │ ├── Medium │ └── Large │ └── States ├── Default ├── Hover ├── Focus ├── Disabled └── Loading
As a project grows, components need controlled changes.
A design-system governance process may include:
A design system should evolve without unexpectedly breaking every page that depends on it.
Create a design system for a technology education platform.
Create a short design-system documentation page explaining how developers should use these standards.

sections.title: LESSON 11 — Building Reusable UI Components and Interface Patterns

blocks.text: A UI component is a reusable piece of interface structure and behavior.
A component should have a clearly defined purpose and predictable behavior.
Consider a website containing 30 different buttons.
Without reusable components, each developer may implement them differently.
A reusable component creates a consistent implementation.
When the button design changes, the component can be updated without individually redesigning every page.
A well-designed reusable component has several important parts.
Visual design, responsive behavior, and interaction appearance.
Configurable values that allow the component to be reused.
Actions or callbacks exposed to the application.
Accessible names, roles, keyboard behavior, and state communication.
Instructions for using the component correctly.

function Button({ children, variant = "primary", type = "button", disabled = false, onClick }) { return ( <button type={type} className={`button button--${variant}`} disabled={disabled} onClick={onClick} > {children} </button> ); } export default Button;
<Button variant="primary" onClick={startLearning}> Start Learning </Button> <Button variant="secondary"> View Courses </Button> <Button variant="outline" disabled> Unavailable </Button>
The component allows different applications to reuse the same underlying button implementation.
The button retains native keyboard behavior and semantics.
A professional button system should define:
A real a element for navigation.
Do not use links for actions simply because they are easy to style, or buttons for navigation when an actual URL is required.

function CourseCard({ title, description, level, href }) { return (
{level}

{title}

{description}

Explore Course
); }
<CourseCard title="Frontend Engineering" description="Learn modern frontend development." level="Intermediate" href="/courses/frontend" />
The same component can display many different courses while maintaining consistent structure.
For a compact navigation, a menu button can expose its expanded state.

function MobileNavigation() { const [open, setOpen] = React.useState(false); return (
Home Courses Resources
); }
This is a simple disclosure-style navigation example.
A production menu should additionally consider closing after navigation when appropriate, Escape handling, outside interactions where applicable, and route changes.
Do not add ARIA menu roles to ordinary website navigation just because it is visually called a menu. The interaction pattern should match the role.
Dialogs are reusable components that display information or request user action.

import { useRef } from "react"; function EnrolDialog() { const dialogRef = useRef(null); function openDialog() { dialogRef.current?.showModal(); } function closeDialog() { dialogRef.current?.close(); } return ( <>

Confirm Enrolment

Do you want to enrol in this course?

); }

This is a starting implementation. A real enrolment action must connect the confirmation to the application's business logic, and the dialog must be tested with keyboard and screen reader interactions.
A reusable input component can standardize labels, instructions, and errors.

function FormField({ id, label, type = "text", error, ...props }) { const errorId = `${id}-error`; return (
{error && (

{error}

)}
); }
<FormField id="email" name="email" label="Email Address" type="email" error="Enter a valid email address." />
This keeps label and error behavior consistent.
The form's validation logic still needs to be implemented separately.
Components should support variations without requiring completely separate implementations.
<Button size="small" variant="primary"> Enrol </Button> <Button size="large" variant="secondary"> Explore Courses </Button>
Use a limited and documented set of variants.
Creating too many variations increases maintenance complexity.
Components have states that affect their behavior and appearance.
For example, a button may be:
State must be represented in the actual component logic rather than only changing the appearance.
For example, a disabled button should use the native disabled attribute when it is genuinely disabled.
Changing only its color or opacity does not prevent interaction.
Composition means building larger interfaces by combining smaller components.

function CourseSection() { return (

Featured Courses

View All
); }
This creates a larger interface from reusable smaller components.
A component API describes how other developers interact with a component.
For example, a Button component may expose:
Button │ ├── children ├── variant ├── size ├── disabled ├── loading ├── type └── onClick
A good component contract should define:
A component should be flexible enough to support its intended use without becoming difficult to understand.
11.15 When Should a Component Be Reusable?
A component is a good candidate for reuse when:
It represents a recognizable interface concept.
Centralized maintenance provides a meaningful benefit.
However, not every small HTML fragment needs its own component.
Premature abstraction can make simple interfaces unnecessarily complex.
Build a reusable UI component library containing:
For each component, document its variants, states, properties, keyboard behavior, and accessibility expectations.

sections.title: PRACTICAL PROJECT — Create a Responsive Design System With Reusable UI Components

blocks.text: Build a reusable frontend design system that can be integrated into a real application.
The project should demonstrate that you can create a consistent visual and behavioral language across different components while maintaining responsive behavior and accessibility.
This is not merely a landing-page styling assignment.
You are developing a small UI system that other frontend developers could use to construct a complete application.
Organize the project into the following sections:
Prefer native dialog functionality when it meets the required interaction pattern.
Important information must not be communicated using color alone.
Create an expandable content pattern containing:
Create primitive, semantic, and component-level tokens.

:root { /* Primitive colors */ --orange-500: #d97706; --black-900: #171717; --white: #ffffff; --gray-100: #f5f5f5; --gray-500: #737373; /* Semantic colors */ --color-primary: var(--black-900); --color-accent: var(--orange-500); --color-background: var(--white); --color-surface: var(--gray-100); --color-text: var(--black-900); /* Spacing */ --space-1: 4px; --space-2: 8px; --space-3: 12px; --space-4: 16px; --space-6: 24px; --space-8: 32px; /* Typography */ --font-body: system-ui, sans-serif; --font-heading: system-ui, sans-serif; /* Radius */ --radius-sm: 6px; --radius-md: 12px; --radius-lg: 20px; /* Interaction */ --duration-fast: 150ms; --duration-normal: 250ms; }
The values above are starting examples. Actual colors and dimensions must be tested for accessibility and product requirements.
Test the design system using these reference viewport widths:
Cards that adapt to their containers.
Dialogs that fit within the visible area.
No content hidden behind fixed navigation.
These are test widths, not mandatory CSS breakpoints.
Use WCAG 2.2 as the primary accessibility reference.

The project structure is a suggested implementation. It can be adjusted according to the framework and team conventions.
Dialogs remain within the visible viewport.
Keyboard users can operate all functionality.
Important information is not communicated using color alone.
Disabled states prevent the intended actions.
Shared design tokens are applied consistently.
Component tokens are documented where necessary.
Light and dark themes are usable.
Shared changes do not unexpectedly break other components.
Final demonstration of the complete UI system.

A website works well at 1440px but overflows at 375px. How would you investigate and fix the layout?
A responsive navigation menu is inaccessible on touch devices because its content appears only on hover. How would you redesign it?
A course card is placed inside a narrow sidebar on a large desktop screen. Why might a container query solve this better than a viewport media query?
A registration form becomes unusable when a user increases browser zoom. Which responsive and accessibility requirements should you investigate?
A dashboard visually rearranges its columns, but the reading sequence becomes confusing. How would you fix the problem?
A custom dropdown works with a mouse but not the keyboard. What functionality and accessibility requirements are missing?
A modal opens visually, but keyboard focus remains behind it. How would you correct the implementation?
A screen reader announces an icon button without describing its purpose. Which accessibility properties would you investigate?
A user submits an invalid registration form, but the only indication is a red input border. How should the error be redesigned?
A dark theme displays white text on a dark background, but some disabled and selected states become difficult to distinguish. How would you improve the token system?
A design-system update changes the size of every button and unexpectedly breaks several pages. How would component contracts and governance prevent this?
A mobile application provides a drag-only interface for rearranging courses. What alternative interaction should be implemented?
An interface contains a large number of dynamically changing notifications. How would you prevent live-region announcements from becoming overwhelming?
A sticky header covers focused controls while users navigate with a keyboard. Which design and accessibility requirements are relevant?
A component library contains many visually different buttons that perform similar functions. How would you simplify the component variants?

Create reusable cards that adapt to their containing elements rather than the viewport.
Build a keyboard-accessible responsive navigation system with clear expanded and collapsed states.
Implement responsive typography and layout sizing with content-driven constraints.
Evaluate a real website against selected WCAG 2.2 success criteria and document improvements.
Create a complete interactive interface that can be operated entirely through a keyboard.
Implement and test buttons, dialogs, status announcements, and form controls with suitable accessibility semantics.
Redesign an interface with contrast, text resizing, reduced motion, and alternative interaction methods.
Build a token-based visual system with component variants and documented interaction states.
Create buttons, cards, navigation, dialogs, and forms with consistent behavior and responsive layouts.
After completing this module, students should be able to develop responsive frontend interfaces that remain consistent across devices and are usable through different input methods.

They should understand how to choose responsive strategies, how to apply accessibility standards, how to structure keyboard interactions, how assistive technologies interpret UI components, and how to build a reusable design system.
Students should also be able to assess a real interface, identify usability and accessibility problems, implement corrective solutions, and document reusable components for other engineers.
Expected outcome: Students should be able to engineer a professional, responsive, accessible, and reusable interface system rather than simply styling individual web pages.
